i18n.en: And Elohim said to Ya'aqov, Arise, go up to Beit-El, and dwell there; and make there an altar to the El who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esav your brother.

paragraphs.commentary: The chapter opens with the deity's command to Ya'aqov to *go up* (*qum aleh*) to Beit-El and build an altar — a deliberate echo of Gen 28:10-22, where Ya'aqov first encountered the deity at this site on his outbound flight from Esav. The phrase *la-El ha-nir'eh elekha b-borchakha mi-pnei Esav achikha* — *to the El who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esav your brother* — names the deity by the Bethel-encounter rather than by the name *YHWH* or *Elohim*; the construction belongs to the patriarchal-El-compound pattern (El Elyon, El Ro'i, El Shaddai, El Olam, El Beit-El, El Elohei Yisra'el) reconstructed by Alt 1929 / Cross 1973 / Smith 2001. The WoH preserves *El* and *Beit-El* in transliteration per the patriarchal-El-compound convention; ASV / KJV *God* and *Beth-el* collapse the compound and obscure the cult-site naming-convention. The chapter's wider editorial frame is the closing of the Ya'aqov-flight-and-return arc inaugurated at Gen 28.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יַעֲקֹב֙ אֶל־בֵּית֔וֹ וְאֶ֖ל כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִמּ֑וֹ הָסִ֜רוּ אֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַנֵּכָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּתֹכְכֶ֔ם וְהִֽטַּהֲר֔וּ וְהַחֲלִ֖יפוּ שִׂמְלֹתֵיכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to his household, and to all that were with him, Put away the foreign elohim that are in your midst, and purify yourselves, and change your garments;

paragraphs.commentary: *Elohei ha-nekhar* (אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר — *the foreign elohim*) is the first explicit Genesis reference to renounced household cult-objects of a class distinct from the *teraphim* of Gen 31:19-35 (Rachel's Aramean household-cult tokens). The phrase inaugurates a recurring Hebrew Bible formula clustered at Josh 24:23-24 (the Shechem covenant — *hasiru et-elohei ha-nekhar asher b-qirbkhem*, with verbal-and-lexical-formula identity to Gen 35:2), Judg 10:16, 1 Sam 7:3, Jer 5:19, 2 Chr 33:15. Modern critical scholarship (Halpern *Emergence of Israel in Canaan*; M. Smith *Origins of Biblical Monotheism* 2001; Albertz *History of Israelite Religion* 1994) reads the formula as evidence of editorially-foregrounded Israelite household polytheism — the formula's presence presupposes the cult-objects' presence. The chapter's Shechem-burial location at v 4 is geographically the same locale as Gen 34's slaughter, raising whether the *elohei ha-nekhar* include Shechemite plunder-gods; the question is documented in the central-glossary entry. The translation preserves *elohim* in transliteration per the central `elohim-as-translation` policy and renders *ha-nekhar* as *foreign*.

paragraphs.text: וְנָק֥וּמָה וְנַעֲלֶ֖ה בֵּֽית־אֵ֑ל וְאֶֽעֱשֶׂה־שָּׁ֣ם מִזְבֵּ֗חַ לָאֵ֞ל הָעֹנֶ֤ה אֹתִי֙ בְּי֣וֹם צָֽרָתִ֔י וַיְהִי֙ עִמָּדִ֔י בַּדֶּ֖רֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלָֽכְתִּי׃

i18n.en: and let us arise, and go up to Beit-El; and I will make there an altar to the El who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me in the way that I went.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתְּנ֣וּ אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֗ב אֵ֣ת כָּל־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַנֵּכָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּיָדָ֔ם וְאֶת־הַנְּזָמִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּאָזְנֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּטְמֹ֤ן אֹתָם֙ יַעֲקֹ֔ב תַּ֥חַת הָאֵלָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִם־שְׁכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And they gave to Ya'aqov all the foreign elohim that were in their hand, and the rings that were in their ears; and Ya'aqov hid them under the oak that was by Shechem.

paragraphs.commentary: *Ha-nezamim asher b-azneihem* — *the rings which were in their ears* — pairs the foreign-elohim with the ear-rings as a single complex of cult-objects to be buried. The qualifier *b-azneihem* (in their ears) explicitly locates these as ear-rings rather than the nose-rings of Gen 24:22, 30, 47 (Rivkah's). The cross-corpus reach of the ear-ring-as-cultic-amulet pattern is editorially significant: Exod 32:2-3 (the golden calf is fashioned from ear-rings extracted from the people's ears); Judg 8:24-26 (Gideon's ephod is fashioned from Midianite ear-rings as spoil); Hos 2:15 [MT 2:13] (the apostate-Israel's ear-rings as cult-paraphernalia). The Shechem-burial-under-the-oak (*tachat ha-elah asher im-Shekhem*) anchors the deposit at the *elonei Moreh* / Shechem-cultic-site complex (Gen 12:6; 35:4; Josh 24:26 — Yehoshua's covenant-stone *tachat ha-allah asher b-miqdash YHWH*). Modern critical scholarship (Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 553-554; Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 241) reads the cluster as an editorially-deliberate redirection of Shechem-area cult-objects.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּסָּ֑עוּ וַיְהִ֣י ׀ חִתַּ֣ת אֱלֹהִ֗ים עַל־הֶֽעָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ סְבִיבֹ֣תֵיהֶ֔ם וְלֹ֣א רָֽדְפ֔וּ אַחֲרֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב׃

i18n.en: And they journeyed; and a terror of Elohim was upon the cities that were round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Ya'aqov.

paragraphs.commentary: *Chittat Elohim* (חִתַּת אֱלֹהִים — *a terror of Elohim*) is the first Hebrew Bible occurrence of the *chittah*-divine-terror motif, a recurring formula naming a divinely-induced collective fear that paralyses or disperses an enemy force without combat. The cross-corpus distribution reaches Exod 23:27 (*et-eimati ashalach lefanekha v-hammoti et-kol-ha-am* — *I will send my terror before you*); Deut 11:25 (the conquest-terror formula); Josh 2:9 (Rachav's report *naflah eimatkhem aleinu*); 1 Sam 14:15 (*chardat Elohim* — the Philistine-camp panic at Yonatan's raid); 2 Chr 14:13, 17:10. The construction *chittat Elohim* (rather than *chittat YHWH*) is editorially distinctive and consistent with the chapter's P-source register, which uses *Elohim* throughout (vv 1, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15). The verse functions narratively to insulate the Ya'aqov-caravan from retaliation for the Gen 34 Shechem slaughter — without recourse to military protection, the divine-terror disperses pursuit.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֨א יַעֲקֹ֜ב ל֗וּזָה אֲשֶׁר֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ כְּנַ֔עַן הִ֖וא בֵּֽית־אֵ֑ל ה֖וּא וְכָל־הָעָ֥ם אֲשֶׁר־עִמּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov came to Luz, which is in the land of Kena'an (the same is Beit-El), he and all the people that were with him.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּ֤בֶן שָׁם֙ מִזְבֵּ֔חַ וַיִּקְרָא֙ לַמָּק֔וֹם אֵ֖ל בֵּֽית־אֵ֑ל כִּ֣י שָׁ֗ם נִגְל֤וּ אֵלָיו֙ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים בְּבָרְח֖וֹ מִפְּנֵ֥י אָחִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And he built there an altar, and called the place El Beit-El; because there the Elohim were revealed to him, when he fled from the face of his brother.

paragraphs.commentary:
The altar-name *El Beit-El* — *El of Beit-El* — extends the patriarchal-El-compound pattern (El Elyon, El Ro'i, El Shaddai, El Olam, El Beit-El, El Elohei Yisra'el) reconstructed by Alt 1929 and Cross 1973. The construction is parallel to Gen 31:13's *anokhi ha-El Beit-El* (the deity's self-identification by the cult-site name); the altar-name at v 7 is the human-side counterpart to the divine self-naming. The central-glossary entry `ha-el-beit-el-divine-self-identification` (which previously applied to GEN-WOH-31:13 only) is here extended to govern v 7.

The construction *niglu elav ha-Elohim* (*the Elohim were revealed to him*) deploys a plural finite verb (*niglu*, niphal 3mp) with *ha-Elohim* as the grammatical subject — one of the patriarchal narrative's grammatically-plural-verb-with-Elohim constructions, parallel to Gen 20:13 *hit'u oti Elohim* (*Elohim caused me to wander*, hiphil 3mp), Gen 31:53 *yishpetu beineinu Elohei Avraham v-Elohei Nachor* (*may the Elohim of Avraham and the Elohim of Nachor judge between us*, qal 3mp), 2 Sam 7:23 *halkhu Elohim* (*Elohim went*, qal 3mp). The grammatical-plural reading is documented in BDB s.v. *Elohim*; HALOT s.v. *Elohim*; the standard modern treatment is Joüon-Muraoka §136a (the plural-of-majesty reading) alongside the genuine-plural reading (Smith *Origins of Biblical Monotheism* 2001).

paragraphs.text: וַתָּ֤מָת דְּבֹרָה֙ מֵינֶ֣קֶת רִבְקָ֔ה וַתִּקָּבֵ֛ר מִתַּ֥חַת לְבֵֽית־אֵ֖ל תַּ֣חַת הָֽאַלּ֑וֹן וַיִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ אַלּ֥וֹן בָּכֽוּת׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And Deborah, Rivkah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Beit-El under the oak; and the name of it was called Allon-Bakhut.

paragraphs.commentary: *Allon-Bakhut* (אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת — *Oak of Weeping*) names the burial-place of Deborah (Rivkah's nurse, last mentioned at Gen 24:59). The verse drops Deborah into the Ya'aqov-caravan without narrative-bridge from her position attendant on Rivkah at Hevron — she has not appeared in the intervening narrative. Modern critical scholarship (Speiser AB pp. 271-272; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 554-555; Hamilton *NICOT* pp. 377-378; Skinner ICC pp. 425-426; Friedman *Bible with Sources Revealed*) reads the verse as a compositional fragment from an older Bethel-Deborah-oak tradition independent of the patriarchal narrative frame. Rivkah's own death is never narrated in Genesis (she is mentioned as buried at Makhpelah only at Gen 49:31, Ya'aqov's deathbed inventory); some scholarship reads the Gen 35:8 Deborah-burial as a displaced fragment of a Rivkah-burial tradition. The Judg 4:5 *tomer Devorah* (palm-of-Deborah of the judge-Deborah), located *bein ha-Ramah u-vein Beit-El* in the same geographical area, suggests a competing Deborah-tradition attached to the Bethel-region tree-cult site. The chapter is editorially dense with cult-site namings (Beit-El, El Beit-El, Allon-Bakhut, Migdal-Eder, qevurat Rachel).

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹב֙ ע֔וֹד בְּבֹא֖וֹ מִפַּדַּ֣ן אֲרָ֑ם וַיְבָ֖רֶךְ אֹתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Elohim appeared to Ya'aqov again, when he came from Paddan-Aram, and blessed him.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּֽאמֶר־ל֥וֹ אֱלֹהִ֖ים שִׁמְךָ֣ יַעֲקֹ֑ב לֹֽא־יִקָּרֵא֩ שִׁמְךָ֨ ע֜וֹד יַעֲקֹ֗ב כִּ֤י אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה שְׁמֶ֔ךָ וַיִּקְרָ֥א אֶת־שְׁמ֖וֹ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

i18n.en: And Elohim said to him, Your name is Ya'aqov: your name shall not be called any more Ya'aqov, but Yisra'el shall be your name; and he called his name Yisra'el.

paragraphs.commentary:
**This verse is the documentary doublet of Gen 32:29 (the Penuel renaming).** At Gen 32:29 the renaming was delivered by the anonymous *ish*-wrestler with an explicit in-text etymology (*ki sarita im-Elohim v-im-anashim va-tukhal* — *for you have striven with Elohim and with men, and have prevailed*). Here at Gen 35:10 the renaming is delivered by *Elohim* directly, without the wrestling-narrative and without the in-text etymology — the formula is bare: *lo yiqqare shimkha od Ya'aqov ki im-Yisra'el yihyeh shemekha*. The two verses report the same renaming twice, with different narrative frames and different agent-designations.

Documentary-critical scholarship treats Gen 35:9-15 as the P-source doublet of the J/E renaming at Gen 32:29: Skinner ICC pp. 422-425; Speiser AB pp. 270-271; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 552-554; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 374-377; Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 (P pericope); Carr *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996. The duplication is the foundational philological problem of the verse. The companion overlay entry `yisrael-second-renaming-beit-el-p-doublet` documents the documentary-doublet phenomenon; the existing overlay entry `yisrael-name-aetiology-sarah-im-elohim` (Gen 32:29) covers the Penuel-etymology proper. Both entries are anchored to the chapter where they are narratively bound; neither subsumes the other.

The Gen 35:9-15 pericope's P-source markers are dense: the *Elohim* register (not YHWH); the *El Shaddai* self-disclosure at v 11 (the P-document's programmatic patriarchal-name per Exod 6:3); the *peru u-rvu* (be-fruitful-and-multiply) covenant-blessing formula (Gen 1:28; 9:1, 7; 17:6, 20; 28:3; 48:4 — P-source signature); the *goy u-qhal goyim* nation-formula echoing Gen 17:5-6 (Avraham's P-source renaming). The dense P-cluster confirms the source-critical reading.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ ל֨וֹ אֱלֹהִ֜ים אֲנִ֨י אֵ֤ל שַׁדַּי֙ פְּרֵ֣ה וּרְבֵ֔ה גּ֛וֹי וּקְהַ֥ל גּוֹיִ֖ם יִהְיֶ֣ה מִמֶּ֑ךָּ וּמְלָכִ֖ים מֵחֲלָצֶ֥יךָ יֵצֵֽאוּ׃

i18n.en: And Elohim said to him, I am El Shaddai: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be from you, and kings shall come out of your loins;

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ani El Shaddai* — *I am El Shaddai* — is the third deployment of the *El Shaddai* divine name in the patriarchal cycle (Gen 17:1, 28:3, 35:11) and the second *ani El Shaddai* first-person self-identification (paralleling Gen 17:1 in form). The *El Shaddai* name belongs distinctively to the P-document register and is the deity's programmatic patriarchal name per Exod 6:3 (*va-era el-Avraham el-Yitzchaq v-el-Ya'aqov b-El Shaddai u-shemi YHWH lo nodati lahem*). The central-glossary entry `el-shaddai` documents the three modern critical etymologies (*shadad* — destroy / Almighty; Akkadian *šadû* — mountain; West-Semitic *Šaddai* class-epithet from the Deir ʿAlla *shdyn*).

*Peru u-rvu* (*be fruitful and multiply*) reactivates the P-source covenant-blessing formula of Gen 1:28; 9:1, 7; 17:6, 20; 28:3; 48:4. The formula's cross-corpus reach is documented in the central entry `peru-urvu`. The pairing *goy u-qhal goyim* (*a nation and a company of nations*) echoes Gen 17:5-6 (Avraham's renaming: *ki av-hamon goyim n'tatikha*) and Gen 48:4 (Ya'aqov to Yosef: *u-n'tatikha li-qhal amim*); the formula names the patriarch's seed as both a single *goy* (nation) and a *qhal goyim* (an assembly of nations) — the patriarchal-promise's federative dimension. The companion *melakhim me-chalatzekha yetze'u* (*kings shall come out of your loins*) echoes Gen 17:6, 16 (Avraham and Sarah: *u-melakhim me-cha yetze'u* / *u-melakhim m'mennah yihyu*). The new central-glossary entry `goy-u-qhal-goyim-nation-company-formula` documents the cross-corpus distribution.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־הָאָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֛תִּי לְאַבְרָהָ֥ם וּלְיִצְחָ֖ק לְךָ֣ אֶתְּנֶ֑נָּה וּֽלְזַרְעֲךָ֥ אַחֲרֶ֖יךָ אֶתֵּ֥ן אֶת־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: and the land which I gave to Avraham and to Yitzchaq, to you will I give it, and to your seed after you will I give the land.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֥עַל מֵעָלָ֖יו אֱלֹהִ֑ים בַּמָּק֖וֹם אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Elohim went up from him in the place where he spoke with him.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-ya'al me'alav Elohim* — *And Elohim went up from him* — deploys the verb *alah* (*go up, ascend*) of divine departure following an encounter. The construction parallels Gen 17:22 (*va-ya'al Elohim me'al Avraham*, following the El Shaddai covenant) — the only other patriarchal occurrence of the exact formula. Cf. Judg 13:20, where the *malakh YHWH* ascends in the flame of the altar at Manoah-and-his-wife. The preposition *me'alav* (*from upon him*) emphasizes a vertical departure-trajectory. The construction is part of the patriarchal-narrative's editorially-load-bearing vocabulary for divine encounter and departure: the deity appears (*niglu*, *yera*), speaks (*dibber*), blesses (*va-yvarekh*), and ascends (*va-ya'al*). The lens-distinctive reading of this physical-vertical-departure vocabulary belongs in the wiki rather than in the translation surface; the philological observation is documented in the central-glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּצֵּ֨ב יַעֲקֹ֜ב מַצֵּבָ֗ה בַּמָּק֛וֹם אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ מַצֶּ֣בֶת אָ֑בֶן וַיַּסֵּ֤ךְ עָלֶ֙יהָ֙ נֶ֔סֶךְ וַיִּצֹ֥ק עָלֶ֖יהָ שָֽׁמֶן׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov set up a pillar in the place where he spoke with him, a pillar of stone; and he poured a drink-offering on it, and poured oil on it.

paragraphs.commentary: The matzevah-and-oil pairing at v 14 is editorially-deliberate as a return-and-elaboration of Gen 28:18 (the inaugural Bethel matzevah-and-oil). The addition of the *nesekh* (drink-offering / libation) is the editorial elaboration: Gen 28:18 had only matzevah-and-oil; Gen 35:14 adds the libation, anticipating the later priestly-sacrificial system. The lexeme *nesekh* (נֶסֶךְ — *drink-offering, libation*) is the only patriarchal libation in Genesis; its cross-corpus reach is in the Mosaic sacrificial system (Exod 25-30; Lev 23; Num 4, 6, 15, 28-29; the festival-calendar libations); polemically (Hos 9:4; Jer 7:18, 19:13, 32:29, 44:17-19, 25; Ezek 20:28); and in the prophetic restoration register (Joel 1:9, 13; 2:14). Modern critical scholarship (Milgrom AB *Numbers* 1990; Levine AB *Leviticus* 1989; Knohl *Sanctuary of Silence* 1995) reads the patriarchal-period *nesekh* as P-redactional anticipation of the priestly cult. The triple matzevah-oil-libation pairing is a distinctive P-elaboration of the J/E inaugural matzevah-and-oil at Gen 28:18.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶת־שֵׁ֣ם הַמָּק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁר֩ דִּבֶּ֨ר אִתּ֥וֹ שָׁ֛ם אֱלֹהִ֖ים בֵּֽית־אֵֽל׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov called the name of the place where Elohim spoke with him, Beit-El.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּסְעוּ֙ מִבֵּ֣ית אֵ֔ל וַֽיְהִי־ע֥וֹד כִּבְרַת־הָאָ֖רֶץ לָב֣וֹא אֶפְרָ֑תָה וַתֵּ֥לֶד רָחֵ֖ל וַתְּקַ֥שׁ בְּלִדְתָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And they journeyed from Beit-El; and there was still some distance to come to Efrat; and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֥י בְהַקְשֹׁתָ֖הּ בְּלִדְתָּ֑הּ וַתֹּ֨אמֶר לָ֤הּ הַמְיַלֶּ֙דֶת֙ אַל־תִּ֣ירְאִ֔י כִּֽי־גַם־זֶ֥ה לָ֖ךְ בֵּֽן׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said to her, Fear not; for now you will have this son also.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֞י בְּצֵ֤את נַפְשָׁהּ֙ כִּ֣י מֵ֔תָה וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִ֑י וְאָבִ֖יו קָֽרָא־ל֥וֹ בִנְיָמִֽין׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, as her nephesh was departing (for she was dying), that she called his name Ben-Oni; but his father called him Binyamin.

paragraphs.commentary:
**This verse carries two load-bearing items: the *nephesh*-departure-at-death formula, and the twelfth-tribe naming-aetiology completing the twelve-sons-of-Ya'aqov pattern.**

*Va-yhi b-tzet nafshah ki metah* — *as her nephesh was departing, for she was dying* — names *nephesh* (נֶפֶשׁ — *life-breath, animating vitality, throat*) as the departing component at the moment of death. The cross-corpus reach: Gen 25:8 (Avraham), Gen 49:33 (Ya'aqov), 1 Kgs 17:21-22 (Eliyahu and the Tzarfat-widow's son: *tashov-na nefesh ha-yeled* — *let the boy's nephesh return*). The formula is the inverse of Gen 2:7 *va-yipach b-apav nishmat chayyim va-yhi ha-adam l-nefesh chayyah* (the conferral-of-nephesh at the breath-inbreathing). The translation preserves *nephesh* in transliteration to maintain visibility for the English reader; the central-glossary entry `tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula` documents the philology and connects to the existing `nefesh-chayah` entry covering the inverse formula. The translation choice avoids ASV *soul*, which carries Platonic-dualist connotations the Hebrew does not.

*Ben-Oni* (בֶּן־אוֹנִי) is grammatically and lexically ambiguous on the noun *on*: (i) *on* I (from *anan*) — *sorrow, mourning, trouble* — yielding *son of my sorrow* (the death-bed reading, contextually supported); (ii) *on* II (from *un*) — *vigor, strength, generative power* — yielding *son of my vigor / virility / strength* (cf. Gen 49:3 Re'uven *bekhori atah kochi v-reshit oni* — *my firstborn, my might, the first of my vigor*; Deut 21:17 *resheet ono*; Hos 12:4; Job 18:7, 12; 20:10; 40:16). The two homonymous roots produce the chapter's deliberate ambiguity (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 245; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 198-199; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 555-557).

*Binyamin* (בִּנְיָמִין) — Ya'aqov's renaming-counter — admits three etymological readings: (i) *ben yamin* — *son of the right hand* (the favored / privileged son; right-hand as the power-position); (ii) *ben yamin* — *son of the south* (cardinal direction; the *yamin*-south orientation of ANE-Hebrew compass-reckoning, with east as the primary direction and the right-hand south); (iii) *ben yamim* — *son of days* (minority reading). The favored-son reading dominates the standard commentaries; the cardinal-direction reading is supported by Albright *BASOR* 99 (1945), Cross *Canaanite Myth* 1973, and Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 245 — the southern-tribe territorial-allocation (Josh 18:11-28) is consistent with the *son-of-the-south* etymology. The naming completes the twelve-tribe-aetiology cluster begun at Gen 29:32 (Re'uven). The Gen 49:27 deathbed-blessing (Binyamin as *z-ev yitraf* — *ravenous wolf*) and the 1 Sam 10:2 *qevurat Rachel* cross-corpus reception are documented in the overlay entry.

paragraphs.text: וַתָּ֖מָת רָחֵ֑ל וַתִּקָּבֵר֙ בְּדֶ֣רֶךְ אֶפְרָ֔תָה הִ֖וא בֵּ֥ית לָֽחֶם׃

i18n.en: And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Efrat (the same is Beit-Lechem).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּצֵּ֧ב יַעֲקֹ֛ב מַצֵּבָ֖ה עַל־קְבֻרָתָ֑הּ הִ֛וא מַצֶּ֥בֶת קְבֻֽרַת־רָחֵ֖ל עַד־הַיּֽוֹם׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov set up a pillar upon her grave; the same is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.

paragraphs.commentary: The Rachel-grave matzevah at v 20 is the only patriarchal-narrative matzevah set as a personal memorial (rather than as a cult-site marker or treaty-witness — the other Genesis matzevot at 28:18, 22; 31:13, 45, 51-52; 35:14 are cult-or-treaty). The 2 Sam 18:18 *yad Avshalom* (Avshalom's monument) is the lexeme's other personal-memorial use. The *ad ha-yom ha-zeh* (*to this day*) editorial-formula assumes a continuing readership able to verify the monument; the formula recurs at Gen 26:33 (Be'er-Sheva), Gen 32:33 (*gid ha-nasheh* dietary rule), Gen 47:26 (Egypt's 20%-tax), Deut 3:14, Josh 4:9, et al. The Rachel-grave site is referenced again at 1 Sam 10:2 (Sha'ul's anointing-itinerary: *im qevurat Rachel b-gvul Binyamin b-Tzeltzach*), placing the traditional site in Binyamin's tribal-territory rather than in the Bethlehem-area; the geographical discrepancy between the Gen 35:19 *b-derekh Efratah hi Beit-Lechem* and the 1 Sam 10:2 Binyamin-territory location is editorially significant (Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 245; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* p. 557).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּסַּ֖ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֵּ֣ט אָֽהֳלֹ֔ה מֵהָ֖לְאָה לְמִגְדַּל־עֵֽדֶר׃

i18n.en: And Yisra'el journeyed, and pitched his tent beyond Migdal-Eder.

paragraphs.commentary: *Migdal-Eder* (מִגְדַּל־עֵדֶר — *tower of the flock*) appears here as a geographical landmark beyond which Yisra'el pitches his tent. The site's location is uncertain: scholarly opinion is divided between a Bethlehem-area pastoral site and a Jerusalem-area landmark, depending on the Mic 4:8 prophetic reception. Mic 4:8 deploys the toponym in a Zion-adjacent eschatological reference (*v-atah Migdal-Eder ofel bat-Tziyyon adekha tete v-ba'ah ha-memshalah ha-rishonah mamlekhet l-vat Yerushalayim* — *And you, Migdal-Eder, hill of the daughter of Tziyyon, to you it shall come — yes, the former dominion shall come, the kingship of the daughter of Yerushalayim*). The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan glosses *Migdal-Eder* as the place from which the Messiah will be revealed; Christian reception (Jerome *Epistle* 108.10) identifies the site with the Shepherds' Field near Bethlehem. The translation preserves *Migdal-Eder* in transliteration per WoH proper-name convention rather than rendering ASV-partial *the tower of Eder* or full *tower of the flock*.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י בִּשְׁכֹּ֤ן יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בָּאָ֣רֶץ הַהִ֔וא וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ רְאוּבֵ֔ן וַיִּשְׁכַּ֕ב֙ אֶת־בִּלְהָ֖ה֙ פִּילֶ֣גֶשׁ אָבִ֑֔יו וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע יִשְׂרָאֵֽ֑ל (פ) וַיִּֽהְי֥וּ בְנֵֽי־יַעֲקֹ֖ב שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָֽׂר׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, while Yisra'el dwelt in that land, that Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Yisra'el heard of it. And the sons of Ya'aqov were twelve.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Three philological items converge in this verse.**

*(i) The deed.* *Va-yelekh Re'uven va-yishkav et-Bilhah pilegesh aviv va-yishma Yisra'el* — *And Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine, and Yisra'el heard*. The deed is narrated without narratorial commentary. Modern critical scholarship reads the v 22a deed-narration as a compositional fragment (Skinner ICC pp. 426-427; Speiser AB pp. 273-274; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 558-559; Hamilton *NICOT* pp. 380-381; Friedman *Bible with Sources Revealed* — E with possible J residue). The deed is retrospectively cursed at Gen 49:3-4, Ya'aqov's deathbed against Re'uven: *Re'uven bekhori atah kochi v-reshit oni... pachaz ka-mayim al-totar ki alita mishkevei avikha az chillalta yetzu'i alah* — *Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the first of my vigor... unstable as water, you shall not have the preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled it — he went up to my couch*. The Gen 49:3-4 explicit-curse confirms the editorial-significance of the v 22 deed.

*(ii) The *piska b-emtza pasuq*.* The MT marks a paragraph-break in the middle of v 22 (the (פ) between *va-yishma Yisra'el* and *va-yihyu b-nei Ya'aqov shneim asar*) — one of approximately 28 such *piska'ot b-emtza pasuq* in the Hebrew Bible and one of the most-discussed instances. The rabbinic reception treats the break as marking the gravity of the deed and Ya'aqov's silence (b. Shabbat 55b; b. Sotah 13a; b. Megillah 18a). The new central-glossary entry `piska-b-emtza-pasuq-masoretic-paragraph-break` documents the masoretic phenomenon.

*(iii) Bilhah's *pilegesh* status.* Bilhah is named here as *pilegesh* (פִּילֶגֶשׁ — *concubine*) rather than *shifchah* (handmaid; her status at Gen 29:29 and 30:3-8 as the mother of Dan and Naftali). The lexeme *pilegesh* names a subordinate-wife status distinct from full-wife (*ishah*) and from handmaid-substitute (*shifchah*); cf. Hagar's status-shift from *shifchah* (Gen 16:1) to *amah* (Gen 21:10) to *pilagshim* (Gen 25:6, Avraham's after-Sarah concubines). The ANE-comparative material (Westbrook *Studies in Ancient Near Eastern Family Law* 1991; Tigay AB *Deuteronomy* 1996; the Hittite Laws on seduction-of-the-father's-concubine; the Middle Assyrian Laws) supports the reading of the deed as a succession-claim power-grab — the firstborn appropriates the father's bed to claim primacy. The 2 Sam 16:21-22 parallel (Avshalom takes David's concubines on the palace-roof at Achitofel's counsel) and the 1 Kgs 2:13-25 parallel (Adoniyah's request for Avishag as a succession-implication, leading to his execution by Shlomo) confirm the ANE-typology. The new central-glossary entry `pilegesh-concubine-status-class` documents the lexeme; the overlay entry `reuben-bilhah-deed-succession-claim-gen-49-retrospective` documents the chapter-specific deed and its Gen 49:3-4 retrospective. The lens-discipline applies: the symbolic-succession-claim reading is mainstream modern scholarship, not WoH-distinctive synthesis.

paragraphs.text: בְּנֵ֣י לֵאָ֔ה בְּכ֥וֹר יַעֲקֹ֖ב רְאוּבֵ֑ן וְשִׁמְעוֹן֙ וְלֵוִ֣י וִֽיהוּדָ֔ה וְיִשָּׂשכָ֖ר וּזְבוּלֻֽן׃

i18n.en: The sons of Le'ah: Re'uven, Ya'aqov's firstborn, and Shim'on, and Levi, and Yehudah, and Yissakhar, and Zevulun;

paragraphs.text: בְּנֵ֣י רָחֵ֔ל יוֹסֵ֖ף וּבִנְיָמִֽן׃

i18n.en: the sons of Rachel: Yosef and Binyamin;

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֤י בִלְהָה֙ שִׁפְחַ֣ת רָחֵ֔ל דָּ֖ן וְנַפְתָּלִֽי׃

i18n.en: and the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid: Dan and Naftali;

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֥י זִלְפָּ֛ה שִׁפְחַ֥ת לֵאָ֖ה גָּ֣ד וְאָשֵׁ֑ר אֵ֚לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁ֥ר יֻלַּד־ל֖וֹ בְּפַדַּ֥ן אֲרָֽם׃

i18n.en: and the sons of Zilpah, Le'ah's handmaid: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Ya'aqov, who were born to him in Paddan-Aram.

paragraphs.commentary: The closing formula *eleh b-nei Ya'aqov asher yullad lo b-Paddan-Aram* — *these are the sons of Ya'aqov, who were born to him in Paddan-Aram* — contradicts vv 16-18 of the same chapter: Binyamin (named in the Rachel-list at v 24) was born *between Beit-El and Efrat* on the journey-south, not in Paddan-Aram. The contradiction is one of the chapter's clearest documentary seams: modern critical scholarship reads v 26 as a P-redactional genealogical-list-fragment harmonized imperfectly with the older J/E Binyamin-birth-narrative (Speiser AB pp. 274-275; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 558-559; Hamilton *NICOT* pp. 379-381; Skinner ICC pp. 426-427; Friedman *Bible with Sources Revealed*). The contradiction has no surface-narrative resolution. The overlay entry `paddan-aram-binyamin-contradiction-documentary-seam` documents the documentary seam and the P-source genealogical-list tradition.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֤א יַעֲקֹב֙ אֶל־יִצְחָ֣ק אָבִ֔יו מַמְרֵ֖א קִרְיַ֣ת הָֽאַרְבַּ֑ע הִ֣וא חֶבְר֔וֹן אֲשֶׁר־גָּֽר־שָׁ֥ם אַבְרָהָ֖ם וְיִצְחָֽק׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov came to Yitzchaq his father at Mamre, to Qiryat-Arba (the same is Hevron), where Avraham and Yitzchaq sojourned.

paragraphs.commentary: *Mamre, Qiryat-ha-Arba hi Hevron* — *Mamre, Qiryat-Arba, the same is Hevron* — is the chapter's triple-toponym identification of the patriarchal-encampment site. Mamre is the patriarchal-encampment-locale (Gen 13:18; 14:13; 18:1; 23:17, 19; 25:9; 49:30; 50:13); *Qiryat-Arba* (*city of four / Arba's city*) is the toponym of pre-Israelite Hevron (Josh 14:15; 15:13, 54; 20:7; 21:11; Judg 1:10; Neh 11:25); Hevron is the standard Israelite-period name. The triple-toponym recurs at Gen 23:2, 19; 35:27; Josh 14:15; 20:7. The site contains the Makhpelah-cave-burial-complex (Gen 23 — Sarah's burial; Gen 25:9 — Avraham's; Gen 49:30-31 — Yitzchaq's, Rivkah's; Gen 50:13 — Ya'aqov's). The translation preserves *Qiryat-Arba* and *Hevron* in transliteration per WoH proper-name convention.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּֽהְי֖וּ יְמֵ֣י יִצְחָ֑ק מְאַ֥ת שָׁנָ֖ה וּשְׁמֹנִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה׃

i18n.en: And the days of Yitzchaq were a hundred and eighty years.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְוַ֨ע יִצְחָ֤ק וַיָּ֙מָת֙ וַיֵּאָ֣סֶף אֶל־עַמָּ֔יו זָקֵ֖ן וּשְׂבַ֣ע יָמִ֑ים וַיִּקְבְּר֣וּ אֹת֔וֹ עֵשָׂ֥ו וְיַעֲקֹ֖ב בָּנָֽיו׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq expired, and died, and was gathered to his peoples, old and full of days; and Esav and Ya'aqov his sons buried him.

paragraphs.commentary:
The patriarchal-generation arc closes with two editorially-significant features: the *zaqen u-s'va yamim* death-formula (*old and full of days*) — covered by the central-glossary entry `zaqen-u-s-va-yamim` which lists the cross-corpus distribution (Avraham at Gen 25:8; Yitzchaq here; David at 1 Chr 29:28; Yehoyada at 2 Chr 24:15; Iyov at 42:17) — and the *reconciled-brothers-bury-father* motif: Esav and Ya'aqov bury Yitzchaq together, parallel to Gen 25:9 where Yitzchaq and Yishma'el together bury Avraham (*va-yiqbru oto Yitzchaq v-Yishma'el banav el-me'arat ha-Makhpelah*). The pattern is editorially-deliberate: the brothers-reconciled-at-the-funeral motif marks the close of each patriarchal-generation transition (Avraham → Yitzchaq with Yitzchaq + Yishma'el; Yitzchaq → Ya'aqov with Ya'aqov + Esav). The new central-glossary entry `reconciled-brothers-bury-father-motif` documents the pattern.

The verse's narrative-position is chronologically displaced: by Genesis chronology Yitzchaq dies twelve-plus years before the Yosef-in-Egypt narrative begins (Yosef is sold at age 17 per Gen 37:2; the Yosef-cycle runs many years before Yitzchaq's natural-death-age of 180 is reached), but the narrative-order places Yitzchaq's death here at Gen 35:29, before Gen 37. The narrative-order versus story-time-order discrepancy is a standard documentary-critical observation (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 246 explicitly notes the chronological-displacement; Speiser AB, Westermann, Hamilton, Skinner concur). The discrepancy is editorially-deliberate: the patriarchal-generation arc must close before the Yosef-narrative begins.
